missing_spec_content.spec_text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. The nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says decay is random (introTips[0]: "Radioactive decay is spontaneous... It just happens randomly."). It never says that decay happens because nuclei are unstable, or that the nucleus becomes more stable by emitting radiation.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Activity is the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays. Activity is measured in becquerel (Bq)
missing_spec_content.why: Activity and its unit, the becquerel, are not taught anywhere. Becquerel appears only as a person's name in the intro.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Count-rate is the number of decays recorded each second by a detector (eg Geiger-Muller tube).
missing_spec_content.why: Count-rate and the Geiger-Muller tube are not mentioned.
The spec lists neutron emission as a fourth type of nuclear radiation. The lesson presents only three types (intro: "three completely different types of radiation").

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to apply their knowledge to the uses of radiation and evaluate the best sources of radiation to use in a given situation.
missing_spec_content.why: Uses are only listed in passing in the intro ("cancer treatments, smoke detectors, carbon dating and nuclear power"). Nothing teaches how to choose or evaluate the best type of radiation for a given use.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.
missing_spec_content.why: Nuclear accidents are not listed as a source of background radiation in keyPoints[3].content.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The level of background radiation and radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location.
missing_spec_content.why: The effect of occupation and location on background radiation and dose is not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv) 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)
missing_spec_content.why: Radiation dose, the sievert and the mSv-to-Sv conversion are not mentioned. Recall of the unit is not required, but students still need to be able to use it.

above_gcse.text: Note: a neutrino is also given out, but you don't need to include it at GCSE.
above_gcse.why: The neutrino is not in the spec. It adds an unfamiliar particle without need.
The neutrino is beyond the spec. Putting it in a bullet to be written down encourages students to learn and reproduce it.
The spec states "The identification of daughter elements from such decays is not required." Polonium is introduced without explanation.

above_gcse.text: Natural sources (~85% in the UK): ... Artificial sources (~15%)
above_gcse.why: Percentage breakdowns of background radiation are not required by the spec.

above_gcse.text: The nucleus is still in an excited state. It releases its extra energy as a gamma ray.
above_gcse.why: Excited nuclear states are not in the spec. The spec only says gamma is "electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus".

factual_errors.correction: Gamma rays have a long range in air (many metres or more), but their intensity falls with distance and absorption. Their range is not infinite.

factual_errors.text: part of the EM spectrum beyond X-rays
factual_errors.correction: The frequency ranges of gamma rays and X-rays overlap. Gamma rays are defined by coming from the nucleus, not by lying strictly beyond X-rays.

The medical share of background-type exposure comes mainly from diagnostic X-rays and scans. Radiotherapy is a targeted treatment dose for individual patients and is not usually counted as a source of background radiation.

wrong_terms.text: It comes from natural and artificial sources.

wrong_terms.spec_term: atomic number / mass number (the symbols Z and A are not used in the spec or defined in the lesson)
